## Design

### 2026-10-20 – # starting with the schematic!

**1.4h**

# starting with the schematic!

After brainstorming a few ideas for what exactly I want in my MIDI, I came up with the following ideas:
* RGB lights that light up when something is pressed
* An OLED screen that will display what key is being pressed
* Making the key switches do something unique, since I'm not sure what they do without the firmware yet
* General appearance customization using silkscreen, edge cuts, and custom key shapes

However, I also don't want to deviate too much from the tutorial because I'm still a beginner, so I made sure to keep things relatively simple. For example, the RGB lights are already included in the guide, so I just used those. The OLED addition is completely new, though I did it with my Starbie so I'm still a little experienced :)

![Screenshot 2026-10-19 234941](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/454291c44a39a37a0aa166a7353786b3b653ba396b2b789c61c8cf6f8fc62908.png)

Here's just what I did for the OLED, which was just connecting everything through a 01x04 Connector Pin. It's the same one from the Starbie project, and making it display text is much easier than making it display images.

This is what my final schematic looks like! I mostly followed the guide for the parts and how to connect everything, though I decided to replace the Rotary Encoder with the OLED (since they use the same amount of GPIO) and add 2 more LEDs (since it uses just 1 GPIO regardless of how many LEDs are placed onto it). When I actually create the PCB and route it tomorrow, I'll make the layout custom to account for everything!

![Screenshot 2026-10-19 234929](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/3ba724ee06765c84aba4ddfbea9a1f8eb0d27df2780c3fbc179498144166b591.png)

tl;dr is that I came up with some ideas for my MIDI and made the final schematic

### 2026-10-20 – # getting the layout!

**2.2h**

# getting the layout!

The most frustrating part of this entry was making the capacitive touch sensors, since they required me to make a whole new footprint and design it in that. I initially already had problems setting up the footprint editor, since I couldn't figure out how to make the pad actually connect to a custom shape. I know the tutorial used a rectangle, and since KiCad already has a preset for that, it would be easy to make a rectangle too. But I really wanted mine to be a star! After lots of googling, I figured out you had to go into the actual editor for a pad by pressing ctrl + e, and I made the first iteration of my keypad. It took a lot of fiddling around, though, to get everything aligned and evenly spaced. It would be so much easier if there was a set aligning tool, but I essentially had to measure everything using lines and the dimension tool. The guide mentioned SPECIFICALLY not to have a messy footprint, so I had to create my own guidelines:

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 213735](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/c44a83964e8df7bd7b040fe7dec1f91c69703b711cf785b39851a31edd899773.png)

To make sure everything was incredibly even, I double checked all the angles and side lengths. Making the rest of the keys was pretty easy, since I only had to duplicate them and assign the polygon to the right pad.

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 214118](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/39bf32431633676535b5df529851ef0b209ac61061687e37dbf40628c4cee4a4.png)

It also took me a while to figure out why the pads/numbers in my stars weren't as big as the one in the guide, before I realized you could edit a pad as a graphic image and just attach the polygon that way. After all that work, I put it into my PCB editor just to realize that it was WAY too small >:(

I thought that KiCad would have a built in scale tool, so I could just scale it up, but for some reason it doesn't. It doesn't even allow you to scale up more complex shapes with more than 4 vertices smoothly, since it just moves each individual point instead of the entire shape. I spent a long time googling to see if there was anything, but I eventually just gave up and redid everything from scratch.

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 222232](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/dfab555b1366e5a207172eff559d9d489a2ea456f0e8a2da2f7198ba838b92b5.png)

Since I made my shape so much bigger, it was much more difficult working with the guidelines, so I had to make a lot more. I also really didn't want to have to do all this again for a third time if it was too big (spoiler alert I had to do it again) so I tried to import it into the PCB editor just to see a general size. I thought it was good, so I completed the rest of the keys, evenly spaced all of them, and updated the PCB from the schematic.

It was then that I realized I had made it way too big. Each star was about the size of one of the keys in the guide, but were spaced too far apart so it looked really awkward. Though, because I already did this twice, the third time redoing it was much smoother.

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 225259](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/0dd810083d7a4cbd43e97df369ffc59af0388eeba88164d820a58da77830a636.png)

I also eventually made the layout for everything, and it was mostly based on the guide's layout, except I replaced the rotary encoder with the 4 pins for the OLED and added the 2 extra LEDs on the front next to the OLED.

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 233637](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/61c7b45b20b86392b065b404245dde253ef7e3a94b6743980ffd7e519cf7eebe.png)

tl;dr is that I spent a long time trying to get the footprint for the keys just right, and I made the layout for my PCB

### 2026-10-23 – # more routing!

**1h**

# more routing!

In the previous entry, I spent a lot of time routing! I mostly finished everything, but I still had some ratlines that I couldn't figure out how to route, since there was essentially no possible way to connect everything and still not have the traces cross over each other. This was because I was working on just the back layer, like the guide told me to, but I had different components and it simply wasn't possible. I first tried using a GND pour to get rid of the GND ratlines I originally had to route, which did help, but I also made sure to get stay away from the capacitive keys like the guide said.

I also eventually discovered that vias existed, meaning that I could just transfer between multiple layers and cross over traces without affecting anything electronically, so I used vias to finish up the rest of my routing!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/7b3c6f4bcb4366c36bd274c5df8c7f15b8aa7828f20cb2cf6888dd16b618fa3e.png)

The other thirty minutes of this hour was trying to figure out the DRC errors that I had, which mostly dealt with how little space I had between each components. This meant that spokes couldn't form because they didn't have enough space, so I had to tweak some traces to give them more room.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/09976fe8defc7dff72b89988c8a064dbce1f479e3c902a3d83bb7b3d1b76cf0d.png)

tl;dr is that I added a GND pour and finished all the routing using vias, as well as fixing all the DRC errors regarding spokes

### 2026-10-23 – # adding some graphics!

**1.3h**

# adding some graphics!

Because my PCB is in the shape of a hexagon, I decided to make my board themed around bees, since the hives they make usually contain hexagons. Because this was a relatively simple step when I made my Starbie PCB, I wanted to try and figure out if I could still add graphics from the knowledge I gained during Week 1 (though it turned out to be a lot more difficult than I recall)

A lot of the time was spent just finding images that I wanted to use on Pinterest, specifically those that were high contrast with clear edges. Though I wanted to use images of real bees on Google, most of those images looked really distorted when put through KiCad's image converter. I also noticed that, for some reason, KiCad's image converter preview doesn't exactly match what the Silkscreen actually looks like on the PCB (at least, in my eyes, it looks darker?), so I originally spent a long time just trying to figure out the exact threshold I needed to make it look right. I gave up eventually because it simply took too long.

Another issue was that I couldn't figure out how to import the kicad_mod file, since the library I had was connected to my Starbie. It took a while before I realized I could just add the library into the MIDI project, and it would work exactly the same!

The most prominent issue was that I couldn't figure out how to change the image from F.cu to F.Silkscreen. There was some labels on the side that looked like this:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/e2437045c2c144ca7d796c5f5911e235b44539bcb3bea62f7613f03cd8604051.png)

However, you're only able to switch between F.cu or B.cu. I Googled it and it told me to look in the Footprint Editor, which I did, but it didn't show. It took me a while of trying to figure it all out before I realized that you need to select individual components rather than the entire footprint before it let you switch the layer to F.Silkscreen. This brings me to another point; KiCad has no scaling function for footprints other than just editing individual vertices, probably the dumbest thing about KiCad. I don't really know why it doesn't have this tool, but people have already been making plugins to solve this issue. My best guess is that footprints are also used for the actual electronic components, and therefore must stay the same size as their real-world counterparts. Though, for this project, I just used a website to scale my footprint up or down.

The text was much easier, since it allows you to switch the layer easier (just make the text on the F.Silkscreen layer). I decided to go with the same convention I did as the Starbie and make the text in Wingdings, and this time it says: "To bee, or not to bee. That is the question." - William Shakespeare

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/d1f3e9e2daf003bdbaf54549119a425c87d1d56d05800846f92664f1764faca7.png)

tl;dr is that I had some issues figuring out how to add Silkscreen graphics, primarily with KiCad's image converter, changing the layer into F.Silkscreen, and changing the size of a footprint

### 2026-10-23 – # setting up for the firmware!

**0.9h**

# setting up for the firmware!

For this project, the guide recommended using KMK for the firmware. I had NO IDEA what that meant, what KMK is, how to set up, how to get started... I was basically going in blind, so it took FOREVER just to figure out what I needed!

I spent some time researching what KMK was and how I could set it up for my MIDI project. Essentially, it's just a way to code firmware for a keyboard specifically without having to make complex code from scratch, since it will use certain tools for certain parts. I didn't really understand it, so I started out by just downloading the KMK zip file from the Github, and the Circuit Python file. Both of them allegedly attest to being beginner-friendly, but I guess I'll see about that...

I had to Google how to set up most of the items, and I realized that you can't really run Circuit Python without having the actual physical microcontroller, so if I wanted to edit it I would just do so in VS Code. The guide comes with a little bit of firmware that I'll use as a base, so I just copied that into a notepad and saved it as a .py file.

I also saved some other files into one folder that Gemini recommended me to have in one folder, including:
* the boot python source file
* the uf2 file for CircuitPython
* the adafruit_midi folder (from a separate Github)
* the kmk folder (from the KMK Github)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/554f70628cc53e7395411ad4f3fc9510410d3a47996d5860da7620e6b9e07758.png)

(The libraries folder contains both the kmk and adafruit_midi folder)

I uploaded everything into VS Code, so then I can finally get started on editing some code to make it fit for my MIDI!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/f8850e542461906a488ad5a0b5a0e55069c311283d5ca37997cdd1c0ad5e7008.png)

tl;dr is that I set up all the files I'll need for making my firmware in VS Code

### 2026-10-23 – # switches and pin numbers

**1.5h**

# switches and pin numbers

After getting my code into VS code, I realized that a lot of the stuff was different in my MIDI than the tutorials'. For one, the pin numbers for my code were completely wrong when comparing with my schematic, so I had to update the pin numbers.

![Screenshot 2026-10-23 215243](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/79cfd0f0199e9a4b8eaa86199b9ac336a7e7b665d6f4f5f063cc264964e28be0.png)

This was the main place that the pin numbers differed (for example, I was using the RX and TX pins for my switches), but I also changed it if it came up later in the code.

Another thing was that I didn't have the rotary encoder, so I had to delete everything that contained  code for that part. The rotary encoder just changes the volume, which I find a bit redundant if you can just change the volume on your computer once the MIDI is plugged in, so I didn't have any problem removing it!

![Screenshot 2026-10-23 214554](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/42b01958d4aa0e00b0222841b68eb7c3a10bde67eb19bbae704879ffada68253.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-23 214517](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/2f1e286f35025939664d5b4c8bd9d7694069818ae0bc90a8a4d87ba1bd314bfb.png)

After that, I had to make sure that I had the libraries for setting up my OLED. It requires 2 libraries, the Adafruit display library and the Adafruit text library, so I had to download those from Github and add them into my main firmware folder.

![Screenshot 2026-10-23 213457](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/7237ae5fe805b92c24d0ba5b57caf84fe08393da9c8231b2ceeeae5bb5385ad7.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-23 213446](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/bf5450ee796a42fa0f61158ae387a6bab2748b3366fcd29af21ee62a39d187da.png)

Then, I started coding the switches. In the tutorial code, the switches are used for playing drum sounds (such as kick, snare, etc.) At this point, I thought that the volume change would still be useful to keep, so I found out how to switch the functions of the switches for volume up/down. I then started going down a rabbit hole of what I could make the switches do, and finally settled on changing the octave up/down! The third switch would still be a kick drum, mostly because it's much easier to add.

To change the octave, you have to use momentary layers (MO) that are created when the button is pressed and removed when the button is released. So, I had to create two seperate layers (1 octave up and 1 octave down) in addition to the original layer. These two seperate layers allow the touch keys to play different notes, which therefore allows different octaves!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/8e56fc248699599f2e1f5b4c910501ab679b6db63563bd4a87324bd8b5ebfd7a.png)

The original keymap is at the top, and the seven KC.MIDI_NOTE refers to the notes of each touch key. The KC.MO(1) and KC.MO(2) refer to making the momentary layers with index 1 and 2 for higher and lower octave. And the KC.MIDI NOTE(36) is for the kick drum. I also made the buttons do nothing (with KC.TRNS) when a higher octave or lower octave is in place, though I'll test and change this later if needed. For the note numbers, I just used this website (+12 for 1 octave higher and -12 for 1 octave lower).
> https://inspiredacoustics.com/en/MIDI_note_numbers_and_center_frequencies
Now I can play melodies on 3 different octaves!

tl;dr is that I set up the pin numbers, added libraries for the OLED, and the firmware for the switches

### 2026-10-24 – # finishing up the firmware!

**1h**

# finishing up the firmware!

The last thing I need to do to get ready for shipping is adding the OLED code to my firmware! It's relatively simple and I think it was a bit easier to understand than the code I did last time. It WAS harder to implement though, so I used Gemini to help me a little bit in order to understand how libraries, KMK, and CircuitPython works (it's a lot easier compared to Arduino C++ since I know at least a little bit of Python). The point is NOT to use Gemini just to copy and paste the code (which defeats the whole purpose of learning), so below is to show my understanding:

The first thing I did was use the busio, terminalio, and displayio libraries that are built into CircuitPython before getting started with the setup for the OLED (which stores all the data and info needed)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/99b5f2885a9ba3a5ddb7324eb89aa917d8c4014a75896bbc514b15fed03524e1.png)

The first line establishes what pins are being used for SDA (data) and SCL (clock), which are GPIO1 and GPIO2 in my schematic. The following 2 lines give the address (0x3C), height/width, and overall tells the computer what is connected to the SCL and SDA pins. (this is basically the same for all 128*64 OLEDs). The "OLED stuff" is the group of indexes that I'll be using so that the computer knows what touch key relates to what note. The note_label just puts on a "-" at the start when no note is playing, and the append shows the note. The note names are the reference group!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/153f5e8224126526f40c4bab033790fb6a8c5894b05dde9d76fd3a3687c460a6.png)

Luckily, the tutorials' firmware already detects what note is being played and gives an index for that note from 0-6, so all I had to do was also change the note_label whenever a certain key was touched (line 37 to 40). Each index relates to a note in the reference group from before. My code just relates this index, and puts in a "-" when nothing is being touched. This is what I mean:
* C is index 0
* D is index 1
* E is index 2
* F is index 3
* G is index 4
* A is index 5
* B is index 6

This means that the screen unfortunately won't differentiate between different octaves, but musically speaking a C is still a C no matter what octave it is on, so I'm still fine with it :)

tl;dr is that I finished up all the firmware by adding in the code for the OLED that will display what note is being played

### 2026-10-25 – # adding a resistor

**0.5h**

# adding a resistor

After talking a little bit with some people on #half-life, I found I needed to add a resistor for the LEDs, especially because I added extra ones. There might be some small current spikes that could be destructive when run through the LEDs, so it's better safe than sorry!

A 330 Ohm resistor works, so I just added that into the schematic. I couldn't find it in the parts, so I just added a standard resistor and changed its value to 330. It should be connected from the GPIO5 pin and the first LED, as all 5 LEDs use the same pin.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/9aa0c68ad406aae1b9c993dd4be53b27cb4f9cb030bb7e7b57628d13394216ca.png)

After that, I updated my PCB in the editor and routed it (which was pretty simple and self-explanatory), but I made sure to keep the resistor close to the GPIO5 pin so the signal's strong.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/81d141a8a92b08d0c34ce5e51765eeebbddc83b2c70e2b40be08e9d831d60273.png)

I also updated everything in my repo and readme to match!

tl;dr is that I added a resistor for the LEDs in order to prevent destructive current spikes
